A connection requires ports that are up and compatible media at both ends. Copper, fiber, and SFP/QSFP modules have distance and speed limits. Having an IP address does not fix a physical failure.
A cable can be connected while the link stays down because a port is disabled or the modules do not match.
Open the connection and compare media, speed, and distance.
Disable a port, test traffic, and watch the link-down events.
Length and media affect propagation and compatibility. Latency, jitter, and loss show the model's result or a scenario condition; they are not measurements of the computer's real network.

Ethernet delivers frames within the local network. The switch learns the source MAC address and the port the frame arrived on. When it knows the destination, it forwards out that port; when it does not, it floods the frame out the eligible ports in the VLAN.
During the first traffic between two computers, the switch may not yet know which port the recipient is on.
Send a ping and check the switch's MAC table.
Repeat the traffic and compare the ports that transmitted frames.
The MAC table is learned from the simulation traffic; it is not filled in from a ready-made result.

The address identifies an interface. The mask separates the network portion from the host portion. Before sending, the device compares the destination network with its own: a local destination is reached directly; any other requires a route, usually through the gateway.
192.168.10.10/24 and 192.168.10.20/24 are on the same network. To reach 192.168.20.10, the first host needs a gateway or a matching route.
Compare IP, prefix, and gateway on the host ports.
Change the mask and see how the forwarding decision changes.
Addresses and routes belong to the lab; the simulator does not use the computer's real network.

To transmit an IPv4 packet over Ethernet, the next hop's MAC address must be known. ARP asks the local network who owns that IP. The reply populates a temporary table. For remote destinations, the gateway's MAC is resolved, not the remote host's.
A PC sending to another subnet asks for the MAC address of the router connected to its LAN.
Send the first ping and open the ARP events that precede the ICMP ones.
